articles.title: Trump Weighs Major Iran Strikes After US Midterms As Approval Ratings Sink
articles.description: The United States is preparing for a possible fresh round of strikes on Iran after the November midterm elections, CNN reported on October 26, citing two US officials familiar with the preparations. According to the report, American forces have been deployed across the Middle East and are ready to launch an operation against Iran within four days of President Donald Trump giving the go-ahead. The proposed campaign would be a significant escalation from Washington's current approach of targeting Iranian infrastructure that can be rebuilt relatively quickly. The officials described the potential operation as a “big effort”, marking a possible shift from the strategy pursued since full-scale military operations were halted earlier this year. Trump Yet To Approve Fresh Iran Strikes Whether Trump will authorise the operation remains uncertain. However, some US officials cited by CNN suggested that the question was increasingly about when, rather than whether, the president would approve the strikes. Most sources familiar with the preparations reportedly expect the operation to take place after the November midterm elections, indicating that Washington may be holding off on a major military escalation until voting concludes. The timing is significant as Trump faces mounting domestic pressure over the economic consequences of the conflict. His approval ratings have fallen sharply ahead of the elections, with public dissatisfaction over the costs associated with the US military campaign emerging as a major concern. Trump's Approval Ratings Fall Amid Iran War Backlash A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on October 26 put Trump's approval rating at 32%, a slight improvement from the previous week's historic low of 31%. A separate survey by the Pew Research Centre found that around 65% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the Iran conflict. Despite the declining numbers, Trump has projected confidence about his ability to decide when the war will end. Speaking at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, he said the conflict would conclude “whenever I want it to end”. “Somebody asked me before, ‘When will the war in Iran end?’ I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end,’” Trump said. He added that the war needed to be concluded properly, with what he described as a “total statement”. Israel Pushes For Joint Military Operation With US Israel is also seeking to resume a joint military operation with the US against Iran, with discussions reportedly under way between the two countries. Earlier this month, Axios reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had been pressing Trump to authorise fresh strikes. CNN's October 26 report also indicated that the Trump administration had asked for the attacks to be delayed. An Israeli official told the network that Netanyahu had attempted to persuade Trump to approve a joint operation before Israel's elections, but the US president had declined to give the green light. “Netanyahu really wanted and tried to convince Trump for a joint attack in Iran before the elections, and Trump did not give a green light,” the Israeli official was quoted as saying. Iran War Costs US More Than $47 Billion The reported preparations for another military campaign come as the financial toll of the conflict continues to mount. As of October 28, the war in the Middle East had cost the US more than $47 billion. With the November midterm elections approaching, the administration faces competing pressures over the timing of any further escalation. While American forces are reportedly positioned to act quickly if Trump approves the operation, the president has yet to publicly confirm whether he will authorise a fresh offensive.

articles.title: US warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after elections
articles.description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — US officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week’s midterm elections in the United States — as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, according to two diplomats briefed on the matter. Both of the diplomats spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment about the sensitive warnings conveyed by US diplomats and defense officials. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats stressed. The president, however, has repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections in the United States are over. Those threats and the fresh US urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation are putting the region on alert that a return to major operations could now be on the horizon. The White House and US officials declined to comment. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran “continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed” and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month — summarily rejected by Trump — that the Iranians still want to see used as the basis to return to a ceasefire. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry issued a statement urging the sides to “exercise wisdom and pursue political solutions to help contain tensions” and prevent a return to full-scale operations in the war that began in late February. The US has told regional allies that the new round of military action could last for several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate — leading to a fight that could last even longer, the diplomats said. The allies have also been urged by US officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response will include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure. It's unclear how soon the US military would be ready While the US has not carried out a strike against Iran since early September, the situation in the Middle East has become more complicated. The conflict has spread, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels carrying out attacks on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure and airports. A Saudi-led coalition has responded with its own deadly attacks on Houthi-held territory in Yemen. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on Gulf nations being briefed to be prepared for potential escalation by the US. It's unclear how soon after Election Day that the US military would be ready to potentially resume strikes. The Pentagon late last month deployed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with a series of amphibious landing ships with Marines aboard — roughly 9,000 troops in all — from San Diego to the Persian Gulf to bolster the US military in the region. At the time, one US official said this deployment could lead to an unusually high naval presence of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines, as well as hundreds of aircraft, in the region, which has only occurred a handful of times in the last two decades. The Navy had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April for the first time since 2003. Trump, who has focused in recent weeks on campaigning for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, has been evasive about what he plans to do next with Iran. The war has proved to be a heavy weight on Republican candidates as they make their case to voters who are fatigued by rising gasoline prices, a byproduct of the war that's driven up costs across nearly every sector in the global economy. The cost of fighting the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to the latest estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. While campaigning for Republicans, Trump has consistently assured voters that the war’s end is near, while also threatening that a new round of bombing could be coming once the election passes. During a campaign stop in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, Trump said a conclusive end to the eight-month-old conflict could be coming “in a couple of weeks, if you don’t mind.” “Somebody asked me before, when will the war in Iran end?” Trump said earlier in the same address. “I said, ‘Whenever I want it to end.’ It’ll be very quick, but we have to have it end properly, with total and complete — a total statement, they will never have a nuclear weapon.” Trump may be looking at a postelection timeline for possible action, but the region is on edge that Tehran could do something provocative before then — especially if they feel U.S. actions is imminent, said Jonathan Schanzer, executive director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. “Why would they wait until after the elections here ... if they could initiate it and potentially gain the upper hand?” he said.
